track: Track E adjacent family and community treatment durability
journal_volume_issue_year: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology 79(5), 2011
article_title: Effects of multisystemic therapy through midlife: a 21.9-year follow-up to a randomized clinical trial with serious and violent juvenile offenders
author: Aaron M. Sawyer; Charles M. Borduin
community_group: 176 serious and violent juvenile offenders originally randomized to multisystemic therapy or individual therapy
page_locator: article pp. 643-652; abstract, methods and results preview, disclosure, and underlying thesis record
source_access: publisher and PubMed primary records, author-supplied article preview, DOI, and underlying thesis metadata inspected
evidence_type: intent-to-treat official-record follow-up a mean 21.9 years after treatment in one randomized clinical trial
exact_factual_observation: Participants averaged 3.9 felony arrests before adolescent treatment. At an average age of 37.3, felony recidivism was 34.8% after MST and 54.8% after individual therapy; misdemeanor offending frequency was reported as 5.0 times lower after MST, and the odds of family-related civil suits were twice as high after individual therapy.
what_source_establishes: A brief adolescent intervention that works across family and community systems can be associated with materially different official criminal and civil outcomes more than two decades after active treatment in the studied trial. A post-treatment window can be long enough to test durability rather than continued service exposure.
what_source_does_not_establish: One developer-led US trial does not establish that MST has the same effect in other jurisdictions, service systems, populations, providers, or comparison conditions. Official records do not measure unreported harm, victim safety, wellbeing, family burden, education, employment, relationships outside court, or the component and transition mechanisms that caused the difference. The result is a group average, not an individual prognosis or screen.
author_interpretation: The authors conclude that MST's positive impact can persist into middle adulthood and discuss policy and service implications.
alternative_interpretation: Treatment attention, therapist or implementation differences, unmeasured post-treatment services and life conditions, record availability outside the searched jurisdictions, or other trial-specific factors may contribute. The extreme duration strengthens outcome persistence while increasing the number of uncontrolled experiences between intervention and measurement.
response_process: Juvenile-court referral; randomized MST or individual therapy; family and community intervention during adolescence; official juvenile, adult-court, police, incarceration, and civil-record follow-up through middle adulthood.
outcome: Lower felony recidivism, misdemeanor frequency, and family-related civil-suit involvement after MST in the intent-to-treat analysis; no direct victim, wellbeing, family-burden, or implementation outcome at the 21.9-year endpoint.
transferability: High for requiring genuinely post-treatment follow-up and official outcomes alongside child and family measures. Medium for the proposition that a family-and-community intervention may have durable effects. Low for direct intentional-community transfer, lay treatment, coercion, or predicting an individual child.
likely_article_destination: Community as therapist / outcome dashboard / child safeguarding / dangerous-child branch
notes: Charles Borduin disclosed membership on the board of MST Associates LLC, which provides MST training for youths with problem sexual behavior. Preserve the developer and single-trial limit; do not infer that treatment response validates admission, membership, or danger screening.

track: Track E adjacent family and home-based child-welfare effectiveness
article_title: Effects of functional family therapy for adolescents in child welfare services on subsequent criminal charges and out-of-home placements: a randomized effectiveness trial
author: Asgeir Røyrhus Olseth; Andreas Høstmælingen; Gunnar Bjørnebekk
community_group: 129 Norwegian youths with registry linkage from a 161-family child-welfare randomized trial
page_locator: complete open article; intake, protocol changes, treatment conditions, Tables 2-3, limitations, funding, and conflicts
source_access: complete open primary article, DOI, trial-registration link, protocol deviations, limitations, funding, and conflict disclosure inspected
evidence_type: randomized effectiveness trial with national-registry outcomes at 18 and 36 months after intake
exact_factual_observation: FFT normally lasted three to six months. Among 129 linked cases, the study found no statistically significant FFT-versus-TAU difference in criminal charges at 18 or 36 months or out-of-home placement at 18 months. Only seven youths were primarily referred for crime and two had prior arrests; 40.7% of the TAU group received MST. The achieved sample could reliably detect only relatively large effects, and confidence intervals were wide.
what_source_establishes: A named family-treatment model cannot be presumed superior to active ordinary services. Context, comparator strength, treatment exposure, population severity, registry linkage, and statistical power can materially alter what a durable-effect study shows. Null comparative results belong in the evidence base.
what_source_does_not_establish: The trial does not prove exact equivalence, absence of smaller benefit, harm, ineffectiveness in juvenile-justice recidivism populations, or ineffectiveness relative to no service. The mixed TAU condition, lower-severity prevention population, protocol changes, linkage exclusions, and limited power prevent those claims. It does not support diagnosis, coercion, or a community-run treatment system.
author_interpretation: The authors conclude that the expected superiority of FFT was not supported and call for more effectiveness research across service contexts.
alternative_interpretation: The active comparator may itself have been effective, particularly because many TAU families received MST or parent training and received more treatment hours on average. Conversely, selection, protocol changes, low event counts, missing identifiers, and limited power may conceal meaningful differences in either direction.
response_process: Child-welfare referral; eligibility and baseline assessment; random assignment; voluntary home- or office-based FFT versus heterogeneous active TAU; fidelity monitoring; national-registry checks at 18 and 36 months.
outcome: No statistically significant between-group difference in criminal charges or out-of-home placement; point estimates favored FFT but wide confidence intervals included no effect and, for some endpoints, clinically important benefit and harm.
transferability: High for requiring an active comparator, service-dose accounting, registry-linkage audit, protocol-deviation record, and uncertainty around a null result. Low for transferring professional treatment authority to an intentional community or extrapolating to serious repeat violence.
likely_article_destination: Community as therapist / outcome dashboard / collective childrearing / dangerous-child branch
notes: The study was funded by NCCBD; Asgeir Røyrhus Olseth and Andreas Høstmælingen were employed by NCCBD, which implemented FFT in Norway from 2007 to 2024. The source concerns mostly disruptive and aggressive child-welfare referrals, not a chronic serious-offender recidivism cohort.

track: Track D adjacent treatment foster care versus group care durability
journal_volume_issue_year: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology 75(1), 2007
article_title: Multidimensional Treatment Foster Care for Girls in the Juvenile Justice System: 2-Year Follow-up of a Randomized Clinical Trial
author: Patricia Chamberlain; Leslie D. Leve; David S. DeGarmo
community_group: 81 girls with serious and chronic delinquency randomized to treatment foster care or community group care
page_locator: article pp. 187-193; CONSORT flow, methods, intervention, models, results, and limitations
source_access: complete open primary author manuscript, PubMed and PMC records, DOI, methods, results, and limitations inspected
evidence_type: intent-to-treat randomized comparison with multi-method delinquency outcomes at 12 and 24 months after baseline
exact_factual_observation: The girls averaged more than 11 criminal referrals at entry and were randomly assigned to MTFC (37) or one of 19 group-care programs (44). The randomized placement averaged 174 days. At 24 months, MTFC predicted a greater reduction in the delinquency construct controlling for age and baseline (standardized beta -0.36, p<.01; Cohen's d 0.65); raw mean locked-setting days differed by 104.82 days in favor of MTFC.
what_source_establishes: A highly trained, supervised family-style placement linked to family-of-origin therapy, school monitoring, daily case data, and on-call professional support can outperform ordinary group care on a multi-method delinquency outcome well beyond the average placement period in this small trial. Peer concentration and transition context are treatment-design variables, not neutral background.
what_source_does_not_establish: The trial does not isolate foster-home structure, peer exposure, caregiver training, family therapy, school attendance, monitoring, or any other component. It does not measure victim safety, family burden, placement coercion, all subsequent services, or later adulthood. A small, mostly White regional sample and developer-affiliated team do not establish independent replication or direct transfer to intentional communities.
author_interpretation: The authors interpret the 24-month findings as maintained efficacy and argue that trained and supervised community foster homes can serve girls with chronic delinquency more effectively than group care.
alternative_interpretation: Differences may reflect the full bundled service, public-school exposure, group-care heterogeneity, peer composition, surveillance and reporting, placement experiences after crossover, or unmeasured follow-on services rather than family-style residence alone.
response_process: Juvenile-court referral; random assignment to MTFC or group care; daily foster-parent monitoring and point system; weekly caregiver supervision; youth and family therapy; school coordination; on-call and psychiatric consultation; blinded 12- and 24-month assessment and court-record review.
outcome: The 24-month delinquency construct and trajectory favored MTFC; days in locked settings had the largest indicator difference. The study reports no victim outcome, no family-burden measure, no direct wellbeing endpoint, and no component-specific causal estimate.
transferability: Medium-high for requiring trained caregivers, independent professional support, family-of-origin and school coordination, explicit implementation review, and post-placement outcomes. Low for unsupervised collective childrearing, community custody powers, or inferring that a household form itself is treatment.
likely_article_destination: Collective childrearing / community as therapist / outcome dashboard / child safeguarding
notes: Adjacent juvenile-justice placement evidence, not intentional-community evidence. The research team developed and evaluated the model; the article itself says the result needs replication.

track: Track D adjacent residential forensic treatment and post-release transition
article_title: Effectiveness of an Individual Cognitive-Behavioral Intervention for Serious, Young Male Violent Offenders: Randomized Controlled Study With Twenty-Four-Month Follow-Up
author: Martin Lardén; Jens Högström; Niklas Långström
community_group: 81 males aged 16-21 convicted of serious violent crimes in five Swedish residential treatment homes
page_locator: complete open article; procedure, intervention, Tables 1-3, post-release results, limitations, and disclosure
source_access: complete open primary article, tables, supplement link, PMC record, DOI, limitations, and conflict disclosure inspected
evidence_type: five-site randomized effectiveness trial with masked interviews and nationwide conviction outcomes at 12 and 24 months after release
exact_factual_observation: Participants received group-based residential TAU, with 38 randomized to an additional 15-to-20-session iCBT module begun four to six months before release and 43 to TAU alone. Only 15 of 38 assigned to iCBT completed at least 15 sessions. Intent-to-treat analyses found no significant added effect on 12-month aggression or 12- and 24-month reconviction. Violent reconviction was 34% versus 23% at 12 months and 50% versus 40% at 24 months for iCBT plus TAU versus TAU; differences were imprecise and nonsignificant.
what_source_establishes: Pre-to-post improvement inside residential care does not establish added treatment effect or post-release durability. Transition planning that names relapse risks and prosocial contacts is not the same as delivered aftercare, treatment completion, or lower reconviction. An active comparator and release-indexed follow-up can overturn an attractive in-program narrative.
what_source_does_not_establish: The underpowered trial and 39% completion rate do not prove that all individual CBT, longer treatment, actual continuing care, or integrated psychiatric, vocational, and social support is ineffective or harmful. Completer comparisons are selected and nonrandom. The sample includes legal adults and cannot be transferred directly to children or intentional communities.
author_interpretation: The authors conclude that this specific brief iCBT add-on was insufficient beyond group-based TAU and argue against further testing in its current format while calling for more comprehensive, integrated, and implementable support.
alternative_interpretation: The null result may reflect a strong and variable TAU comparator, insufficient dose, weak integration, treatment dropout, implementation limits, low power, or contamination within shared sites. The direction of intent-to-treat point estimates also means benefit cannot be assumed merely because completers looked better.
response_process: Serious violent conviction; baseline and trained independent assessment; site-balanced randomization; residential TAU with or without weekly individual CBT; relapse planning and identification of prosocial supports; therapist supervision; pre-release posttest; masked 12-month interview; nationwide conviction follow-up through 24 months.
outcome: Both groups improved on several in-residence self-reports, but no significant added iCBT effect appeared after release on aggression or violent or any reconviction. Nationwide registry outcomes were complete; interview outcomes were not.
transferability: High for indexing follow-up to release, measuring completion and implementation, using an active comparator, and keeping in-program change separate from post-release outcomes. Low for generalizing this module to other CBT, children, community governance, or a danger screen.
likely_article_destination: Outcome dashboard / durable transition / community as therapist / dangerous-child branch
notes: The first author designed the iCBT module but declared no commercial or financial relationship and no royalties, training, or consulting gain. Do not use completion, diagnosis-oriented measures, SAVRY ratings, or convictions as automatic membership or punishment criteria.
